Abstract
Omni-modal dialogue models can understand
multimodal inputs and synthesize spoken
replies, yet their responses remain visually dis-
embodied. We introduce Ex-Omni-2D, an
omni-modal dialogue framework that generates
a coordinated response comprising text, person-
alized speech, and reference-conditioned video.
Given a multimodal query, reference image,
and reference audio, the model predicts a struc-
tured Visual Thought Plan (VTP) describing
scene, emotion, and motion, followed by re-
sponse text and native multi-codebook speech
units. These units form a shared acoustic-
temporal interface: they are decoded into
speech and aligned online with video frames.
This interface enables the response and avatar
pathways to be learned from heterogeneous
speech, dialogue, and avatar-video data, avoid-
ing the need for large-scale query–text–speech–
video supervision. A full-sequence Video Gen-
erator serves as the primary Teacher. For effi-
cient incremental generation, we further distill
it into a few-step block-causal Streaming Stu-
dent whose Prefix Streaming mechanism car-
ries a clean latent across consecutive chunks
to reduce cumulative late-chunk degradation.
With four-step inference, the complete four-
GPU pipeline achieves an end-to-end RTF of
1.293 at 400×720/720×400, providing a prac-
tical quality–efficiency operating point.

The dialogue model first produces a structured Vi-
sual Thought Plan (VTP) describing scene, emo-
tion, movement style, and motion details, followed
by the user-facing response. It then generates native
multi-codebook speech units as a shared acoustic-

video frames, coupling vocal content and avatar
motion without requiring a completed waveform.
This factorization is motivated by data availability
rather than by treating video as a post-hoc add-

speech-centric supervision, whereas the avatar path-

VTPs and teacher-forced speech units. At inference
time, the dialogue-derived VTP and generated unit
stream reconnect the separately supervised path-
ways. Thus, the framework obtains a coordinated
response without assuming large-scale dialogue ex-
amples paired with target response videos.
The Video Generator has two realizations. A
full-sequence Teacher provides the primary visual
realization and is conditioned on reference appear-
ance, VTP semantics, and frame-aligned speech
units. For efficient deployment, we distill it into
a few-step block-causal Streaming Student. We
adopt AnyFlow’s flow-map and on-policy distilla-
tion objectives (Gu et al., 2026); our contribution
is to integrate them with an avatar-specific stream-
ing state and introduce Prefix Streaming. Each
post-initial window carries one detached clean la-
tent from the preceding chunk as a temporal prefix
for three new latents, while maintaining chunk-
aligned speech conditioning. This design reduces
cumulative late-chunk subject degradation without
repeating output frames. The Student provides an
efficiency-oriented alternative, while the Teacher
remains preferred when visual quality is the pri-
mary objective.
Experiments across multiple benchmarks char-
acterize dialogue, speech, video, audio–video syn-
chronization, and efficiency performance. The full-
sequence Teacher and incremental Student provide
complementary quality- and efficiency-oriented op-
erating points.

dialogue, and avatar-video data without fully
paired video-response dialogues.
• We distill the full-sequence Teacher into a
block-causal Streaming Student and introduce
Prefix Streaming to reduce cumulative late-
chunk subject degradation while enabling effi-

4 Experiments
4.1 Evaluation
Benchmarks and reference conditions. We
conduct the audio-video evaluation on the
CommonEval question-answering test set from
VoiceBench (Chen et al., 2024a), which contains
200 speech queries. Because Ex-Omni-2D requires
a reference image and reference audio, we sam-
ple paired reference conditions from the held-out
SpeakerVid test split (Zhang et al., 2025b). For
each CommonEval query, the reference image and
reference speech are held fixed across all compared
methods; a baseline consumes only the modalities
supported by its interface. For spoken question
answering, we use AlpacaEval, CommonEval, and
BBH from VoiceBench. For multi-turn dialogue
quality, we use the 400-dialogue OmniCharacter
benchmark (Zhang et al., 2025a) and follow its
official CharacterEval protocol.
Metrics. We evaluate audio-video generation in
terms of audio quality, video quality, and A-V
Sync. For audio quality, we report Production
Quality (PQ) and Content Usefulness (CU) from
AudioBox (Tjandra et al., 2025), together with
speaker similarity (SIM) under the Seed-TTS evalu-
ation protocol (Anastassiou et al., 2024). For video
quality, we report Subject Consistency (SC), Imag-
ing Quality (IQ), and Dynamic Degree (DD) from
VBench (Huang et al., 2024). DD is a descriptive
measure of substantial motion rather than a mono-
tonic measure of motion naturalness or semantic
correctness. For A-V Sync, we report SyncNet
confidence (Sync-C; higher is better), which mea-
sures lip-speech synchronization. Spoken ques-
tion answering is scored using the open-source
VoiceBench evaluation code. For OmniCharacter,
we report all twelve official dimensions and their
unweighted average, while highlighting Fluency,
Coherency, and Consistency as the conversational-

4.7 Comparison with No-Prefix Streaming
Figure 4 compares our earlier no-prefix Stream-
ing Student with the Prefix-Streaming Student us-
ing both representative later-chunk examples and
full-set temporal curves. In the examples, condi-
tioning only through the causal cache produces
visible facial or body degradation in later chunks,
whereas the one-prefix-plus-three-new-latent de-
sign reduces these failures. This comparison com-
plements the cache analysis in Section 3.5: cached
history alone is not equivalent to placing the pre-
ceding clean latent inside the current denoising
window.
For the full-set comparison, both systems are in-
dependently selected on validation data after train-
ing with their respective streaming constructions;
this is therefore a comparison of the two selected
Student systems rather than an inference-time pre-
fix toggle on one checkpoint. Across all 200 Com-
monEval samples, Prefix Streaming changes SC
from 92.85 to 93.65, IQ from 55.18 to 57.40, and
Sync-C from 3.69 to 3.90, while both variants ob-
tain the same DD of 32.00. The 16-chunk DINO
analysis increases mean chunk subject consistency
from 0.9251 to 0.9319, reduces the consistency-
error slope from 0.00783 to 0.00599 per chunk,
and lowers last-minus-first consistency error from
0.1005 to 0.0790, a 21.4% reduction. Prefix is
mixed during the first eight chunks but is higher at
every chunk from 9 through 16, with all paired 95%
confidence intervals excluding zero. These results
support the specific claim that Prefix Streaming
reduces cumulative late-chunk subject degradation.

spans.content: 5 Conclusion
We presented Ex-Omni-2D, an expressive omni-
modal dialogue framework with dialogue-native
video responses. Reference image and reference
audio provide appearance and voice conditions, a
structured Visual Thought Plan makes response-
specific visual intent explicit, and a native multi-
codebook speech space supports both speech ren-
dering and frame-aligned avatar motion. The
modality-specific realization pathways are trained
separately because large-scale dialogues paired
with target response videos are difficult to ob-
tain; VTP and speech units reconnect them within
the response process. The full-sequence Teacher
provides the primary video realization, while the
Prefix-Streaming Student transfers the same re-
sponse interface into a few-step causal generator
for incremental output. The two models expose
complementary quality- and efficiency-oriented op-
erating points.
Limitations
Although Ex-Omni-2D generates intelligible
speech, its similarity to the reference speaker still
leaves room for improvement. VTP provides high-
level semantic guidance rather than an indepen-
dently sufficient video-control signal: the final re-
alization is jointly conditioned on the plan and
frame-aligned speech units, and a fixed balance
between Text CFG and Audio CFG may not trans-
fer uniformly across responses. Generating VTP in
the shared autoregressive channel also introduces
a measurable speech-QA and reasoning trade-off,
motivating future planner isolation and adaptive
cross-modal guidance. Our long-horizon analysis
is limited to temporal subject stability and facial-
motion regularity. The full-sequence Teacher re-
mains computationally expensive because it uses
bidirectional temporal context and a large denois-
ing budget. The Streaming Student substantially
improves video throughput and enables incremen-
tal generation, but it reports lower IQ, DD, and
Sync-C than the Teacher under the evaluated set-
tings. Moreover, its first playable video chunk ar-
rives after 3.142 seconds and its single-request E2E
RTF remains above 1 in our four-GPU pipeline,
so streaming should be understood as incremen-
tal output rather than end-to-end real-time interac-
tion. Scaling the causal video backbone, reducing
response-planning latency, and improving few-step
distillation may narrow these gaps. Accordingly,
the Streaming Student is an efficiency-oriented de-
ployment path rather than a replacement for the
full-sequence Teacher.

A Evaluation Metric Details
Audio metrics. We use AudioBox-Aesthetics
(Tjandra et al., 2025) to evaluate generated speech
with PQ and CU. PQ focuses on perceptual produc-
tion quality, reflecting whether the audio sounds
clear, natural, stable, and free of obvious artifacts.
CU evaluates the practical usefulness of the gen-
erated content, emphasizing intelligibility and se-
mantic completeness. Compared with strict word-
error-rate matching, CU better captures whether
the generated speech is usable and understandable
from a listener’s perspective. We additionally re-
port SIM using the official Seed-TTS evaluation
protocol: WavLM-Large (Chen et al., 2021) and an
ECAPA-TDNN (Desplanques et al., 2020) speaker-
verification head embed the generated and refer-
ence speech, and SIM is their cosine similarity.
Video metrics. We use VBench (Huang et al.,
2024) to evaluate generated videos with SC, IQ,
and DD; none of these metrics requires a ground-
truth video. SC measures the temporal consistency
of the generated subject, IQ measures perceptual
frame quality such as sharpness and visible arti-
facts, and DD uses optical-flow magnitude to report
the proportion of videos with substantial motion.
A-V Sync. We use SyncNet confidence (Sync-C)
(Chung and Zisserman, 2016; Prajwal et al., 2020)
to evaluate whether mouth movements are tempo-
rally aligned with the generated speech. Sync-C
measures the separation between the best audio-
video alignment and competing temporal offsets,
so higher values indicate more confident synchro-
nization.
Speech QA metrics. For spoken question an-
swering, we use AlpacaEval (Li et al., 2023), Com-
monEval (Chen et al., 2024a), and BBH (Suzgun
et al., 2022) from VoiceBench (Chen et al., 2024a)
and follow the open-source VoiceBench evalua-
tion code. AlpacaEval and CommonEval use GPT-
4o-mini to judge open-ended response quality on
a five-point scale, where 5 is the best score; Al-
pacaEval emphasizes general instruction following,
whereas CommonEval focuses on common spoken
QA. BBH evaluates complex QA requiring multi-
step reasoning, logical composition, and abstract
thinking, and is reported as accuracy. Each BBH
subtask then applies task-specific string match-
ing or regular expressions to convert free-form re-
sponses into binary labels, such as yes/no answers,
option choices, navigation decisions, truthfulness
judgments, or sports-plausibility judgments. The
final score is computed as the percentage of correct
predictions.
B Additional Dialogue Capability Results
Effect of VTP supervision. We isolate the effect
of training the LLM to emit the structured VTP be-
fore its user-facing response. As shown in Table 7,
response-only training without VTP supervision
obtains 3.82 on CommonEval and 61.10 on BBH.
Adding VTP supervision changes these scores to
3.71 and 58.70, corresponding to decreases of 0.11
and 2.40 points, respectively. This is a measurable
language-capability trade-off rather than a uniform
preservation result: the shared autoregressive chan-
nel gains an explicit visual-planning interface at
the cost of lower speech-QA and reasoning scores.
Separating or parameter-isolating the planner may
reduce this interference in future work.

target video. We do not regard these records as

L.2 Framework Training and Student
Distillation
Stage 1: Speech Interface Alignment. We first
use approximately 800K ASR and 1M TTS exam-
ples to establish the bidirectional speech interface
while freezing the LLM, Speech Encoder, and Vi-
sion Encoder. ASR batches update the Speech
Projector, grounding speech inputs in the LLM rep-
resentation space. TTS batches update the Qwen3-
TTS-initialized (Hu et al., 2026) Speech Generator,
teaching it to predict native multi-codebook units
from response-side representations. Thus, Stage 1
updates the Speech Projector and Speech Genera-
tor, with each batch activating only the branch for
which it provides supervision.
Stage 2: Omni-modal Response Adaptation.
We then jointly update the LLM, Speech Projec-
tor, and Speech Generator using examples from
InstructS2S-200K (Fang et al., 2025a) and Om-
niCharacter (Zhang et al., 2025a). The LLM learns
the structured <thinking>–<response> protocol,
where the thinking block contains the VTP, while
speech supervision remains restricted to the re-
sponse span. This stage adapts the aligned
speech interface toward interactive and character-
consistent spoken replies without requiring a target
response video.
Stage 3: Avatar Video Realization. Finally, we
train the full-sequence avatar diffusion model on
the 140K SpeakerVid-derived records described
above. Each training example provides a reference
image, an automatically annotated VTP, teacher-
forced multi-codebook speech units, and a tar-
get video. The diffusion model is therefore op-
timized to realize the same semantic and acoustic-
temporal interfaces that the response pathway pro-
duces at inference time. Importantly, this stage
does not assume that the source clips are dialogue
responses and does not introduce synthetic user
queries merely to label them as dialogue data. The
interface-based decomposition is what permits the
response and video pathways to use their respective
data sources: dialogue supervision teaches what to
say and how to plan a response, whereas Speak-
erVid supervision teaches how to render a supplied
plan and speech-unit sequence as video.

is frozen as the Teacher. Stage 4 trains the
Streaming Student in two successive phases rather

the Teacher, and Phase II performs on-policy chun-
ked Student rollouts with distribution matching
while retaining the flow-map objective. This hier-

distinct from the deployment-oriented distillation
procedure. The data sources and trainable modules
of each stage are specified in the stage descriptions
above and the implementation paragraph below.
For the video pathway, Stage 3 uses 125-frame
SpeakerVid clips assigned to three 720p aspect-
ratio buckets, while both Stage 4 phases use 121-
frame windows with the same buckets.
